extracted.intended_audience: novelists, students of fiction, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_short: novel method and point of view
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the methods by which a novelist selects, arranges, and presents material — including point of view, scene construction, and the choice between pictorial and dramatic treatment — illustrated from Flaubert's Madame Bovary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single subject / unity of meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The book should have a single, clear subject — 'Flaubert has only one word to say' and 'the subject stands firm and clear, without the least shade of ambiguity.' The novel should be a single image rather than a mere row of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and maintain a coherent central idea or image; facts have no validity until used to announce the meaning the author sees. Avoid diffusing the book with multiple competing subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show rather than tell (fiction must look true)
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel must 'look true' by internal means, not by attestation to external authority; mere statement of facts is 'no more than to state the “argument” of the book.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on outside claims of truthfulness; use the book's presentation — scenes, detail, viewpoint — so the story appears true to the reader. Avoid treating narrative as mere information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of information / method as choosing a path
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist's method is 'his manner of choosing his path' — how he selects which facts to offer and how to place them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be deliberate in what you reveal and when; criticism can focus on how information is selected and ordered. Different selections produce distinct artistic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenic vs panoramic presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between a 'scenic' presentation (a particular scene, a single hour) and a 'panoramic' presentation (sweeping, surveying a stretch of time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to place the reader in immediate presence of an incident or to provide a wide-range summary; alternate or combine methods only with purpose. Maintain intelligible contrast between these manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial (subjective) vs dramatic (objective) treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene may be treated pictorially—rendered through a character's receptive consciousness and mood—or dramatically—objective, as if placed on stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose treatment according to desired effect: pictorial for mood-coloured impressions (e.g., Emma's experience), dramatic for objective presentations where visible facts carry the impression. Mixing is allowed but should be managed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view / centre of vision
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine 'with which of the characters, if with any of them, is the writer to identify himself' — i.e., whose mind will interpret the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a central consciousness when possible and avoid haphazard plunges into other minds; unnecessary shifts of focus confuse the effect. Use other centres only when the subject requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial voice vs impersonality (dramatizing opinion)
rubrics_metrics.description: An author may appear 'impersonal' by suppressing direct comment, but his judgment is shown through dramatization; sometimes the author speaks with his own voice, sometimes through a character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express judgments tactfully through scenes and character rather than direct statement; whether you adopt an impersonal stance or a visible authorial voice, be consistent in how opinion is embodied.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to supply background or inner knowledge (authorial intervention)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author must sometimes 'intervene with his superior knowledge' to recall past circumstances or enter characters' consciousness where spectators could not infer them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide additional information or interiority only when necessary for understanding; such interventions should illuminate the drama rather than intrude gratuitously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding haphazard interior plunges
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Haphazard and unnecessary plunges into the inner life of the characters only confuse the effect, changing the focus without compensating gain.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit shifts into interiority to moments of clear purpose; ensure each internal reveal compensates the change of focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of method / following a principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The only law that binds the novelist is 'the need to be consistent on some plan... to allow himself no more latitude than he requires.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a coherent plan or set of principles for treatment and stick to them; inconsistency in method weakens the work's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene placement and preparation (necessity of scenes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene 'that is not really wanted, and that does nothing in particular... is a weakness' — scenes should be placed where everything is ready for their opportunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure scenes are prepared by prior material and serve a clear function (start interest, raise a question, or achieve climax). Cut or revise scenes that fail to contribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of scenes as structural articulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes form 'the articulation of the book, the scheme of its structure' — key episodes (ball, cattle-show, theatre, interview, deathbed) define stages of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribute scenes to guide the reader through stages of development; let each scene establish an aspect of the subject and lead toward the next stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method depends on subject; subject determines treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer's method 'depends upon the particular story he is engaged in telling' — the subject asks for the kind of treatment congenial to the writer's hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the chosen subject and its requirements shape choices of POV, presentation, and devices rather than forcing a preconceived method onto incompatible material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facts are instruments, not ends
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'facts have no validity in themselves, they are nothing until they have been used' — events and incidents illustrate the subject rather than constitute it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use incidents to illuminate the central idea; avoid treating plot events as inherently meaningful without tying them to the book's larger purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of language and deliberate craftsmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist 'weighs every word and calculates every effect so patiently' — craft requires measured choice, not casualness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work deliberately at language and effect; don't choose a method for convenience. Rework until words and arrangements convey the intended impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternation and fusion of methods (layering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods are 'few and simple, but infinite in their possibilities of fusion and combination' — dramatic action may be treated pictorially, viewpoints blended, methods layered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explore combining methods to enrich treatment, but do so consciously and with attention to the principle that governs their mixture so the result remains coherent.
